tldr: This paper reveals a new supply chain vulnerability in robot simulators called Collision Mesh Poisoning (CMP). In a 3D asset, the visual mesh (for rendering) and collision mesh (for physics) are decoupled. By stealthily tampering only with the collision mesh, an attacker creates policies that perform flawlessly in simulation but fail catastrophically upon real-world deployment.
hero_caption: Overall concept of the Collision Mesh Poisoning (CMP) attack. While the rendering visual mesh remains untouched, only the collision mesh used for physics simulation is maliciously altered. The trained policy achieves high success inside the simulator, but immediately fails to grasp and drops objects once deployed in the physical world.
overview:
Training robotic manipulation policies via reinforcement learning directly on physical hardware is often prohibitively expensive and risky, making robot simulators the industry de facto standard. Inside simulators, 3D assets consist of two distinct geometries: a visual mesh used for rendering and a collision mesh used by physics engines for contact detection. To reduce computational overhead, simplifying collision meshes into coarse approximations (e.g., via convex decomposition) is a legitimate and standard practice. The authors designate this discrepancy the Visual–Collision Gap (V–C Gap).

However, the authors discovered that this ubiquitous gap opens up a severe and practical attack surface. An attacker leaves the visual mesh untouched and subtly distorts only the collision mesh before distributing it via public repositories, thereby poisoning the policies of unsuspecting developers. This is Collision Mesh Poisoning (CMP). Inside the simulator, the policy learns contact dynamics based on the poisoned collision boundary and is evaluated on the exact same asset, resulting in a near-perfect simulation success rate. Yet the moment it interacts with genuine real-world geometry, the robot misjudges contact timing and positioning, triggering grasp failures, dropped objects, and physical damage.

The authors developed a black-box optimization framework capable of automatically synthesizing poisoned collision meshes without any knowledge of the victim's learning algorithms or policy architectures. Evaluated in both simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, CMP maintained high simulation stealth while causing physical success rates to plummet by an average of 61.67 percentage points. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that standard geometric anomaly detection and vision-language model (VLM) inspections fail to defend against CMP, raising a critical alarm across the robotics development ecosystem.
contributions: Identified for the first time that the legitimate Visual–Collision Gap (V–C Gap) in robot simulators introduces a novel supply chain attack surface.

Formulated a black-box optimization framework that synthesizes collision meshes balancing stealth in simulation with physical harm in reality, without needing access to victim policy architectures or training algorithms.

Demonstrated attack efficacy across multiple simulation tasks and real-world Franka Panda experiments, proving significant real-world performance degradation while maintaining high simulation success rates.
Evaluated defense mechanisms based on geometric statistical indicators and state-of-the-art VLMs, revealing the limitations of current inspection approaches against CMP.

sections.heading: An Invisible Lie: A New Threat Lurking Between Simulation and Reality
sections.summary: The paper introduces Collision Mesh Poisoning (CMP), a supply chain attack exploiting the decoupling of visual rendering and collision computation in 3D simulator assets. It outlines the threat model and the mechanism through which policies secretly fail once deployed in the real world.
sections.details:
Simulators are an indispensable infrastructure in learning-based robotic manipulation due to physical safety constraints and data collection costs. Inside modern simulators, 3D assets maintain separate representations: a visual mesh defining appearance and a collision mesh handling contact dynamics. Computing contact mechanics on dense visual meshes is computationally intractable; thus, approximating collision meshes via convex decomposition is a legitimate and widespread engineering practice. The authors define this geometric divergence as the Visual–Collision Gap (V–C Gap).

Previously, this discrepancy was examined exclusively as a source of Sim-to-Real degradation, completely overlooking its cybersecurity implications. Consider an attacker uploading a 3D asset with an unaltered visual mesh but a poisoned collision mesh to a public asset platform using an ordinary account. Current asset vetting routines focus on malware scanning, copyright compliance, and format validation, entirely ignoring visual-collision consistency.

When a developer uses this asset to train a reinforcement learning policy, the policy adjusts its contact motions to the corrupted collision boundary. Because simulation validation is conducted within the same poisoned environment, training and evaluation logs reflect stellar performance (stealth). However, the moment the policy is deployed to a real robot, the mismatch between the poisoned boundary and true physical geometry causes severe physical harm, such as dropped objects, tip-overs, or liquid spillage. The authors frame this dual-objective challenge through black-box optimization and confirm its viability in both simulation and physical hardware.

captions.F2: Typical internal structure of a 3D asset within a robot simulator. A single object maintains completely decoupled representations: a visual mesh for rendering and a collision mesh for physics and contact computation. CMP surgically targets only this collision mesh.

sections.heading: 3D Asset Supply Chains and Vulnerabilities in Learning-Enabled CPS
sections.summary: This section examines the 3D asset supply chain landscape in robot simulators. It differentiates CMP from traditional adversarial and data poisoning attacks, highlighting why CMP is both practical and exceptionally challenging to defend against.
sections.details:
### 2.1 3D Assets in Robot Simulation
In a simulated 3D asset $A=(V,C)$, the renderer references visual mesh $V$, while the physics engine evaluates collision mesh $C$. While simulators offer fallback automatic convex decomposition directly from visual meshes, automated geometry-only decomposition frequently destroys fine contact features required for manipulation. Consequently, simulators prioritize pre-tuned collision meshes provided within the asset package. This architecture grants asset distributors virtually full control over the underlying collision geometry.

### 2.2 3D Asset Supply Chain
An audit of official simulation repositories and open data hubs revealed thousands of third-party assets with cumulative downloads reaching the millions. Assets uploaded by anonymous individual accounts frequently accumulate tens of thousands of downloads, enabling attackers to distribute poisoned assets easily through standard, legitimate supply chain avenues.

### 2.3 & 2.4 Attacks against Learning-enabled CPS and Data Poisoning
Conventional cyber-physical system (CPS) attacks typically focus on deployment-time physical patches or training-time backdoor modifications to reward functions, loss formulations, or model weights. However, placing physical patches in restricted spaces like automated factories or hacking into private training pipelines requires unrealistic assumptions. Unlike standard machine learning data poisoning that alters labels or training samples, CMP poisons the physical contact boundaries generated by the simulator. It compromises the policy indirectly through the supply chain without ever breaching the victim's training infrastructure.

sections.heading: Threat Model and the Dilemma Between Stealth and Harm
sections.summary: The authors formalize a strict black-box threat model where the attacker has no insight into the victim's policy architecture or learning pipeline. The attack is framed as an optimization problem balancing the trade-off between high simulation success and real-world failure.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Threat Model
The victim developer downloads simulation assets from a public hub, trains and verifies a manipulation policy in simulation, and subsequently deploys it onto physical hardware. The attacker takes an original asset $A_i=(V_i, C_i)$, preserves $V_i$ exactly, modifies only the collision mesh into $C_i'$ to create $A_i'=(V_i, C_i')$, and uploads it from a regular account. The attacker has zero knowledge of the victim's neural architecture, observation space, or training algorithms (a strict black-box setting).

Although task details are hidden from the attacker, basic manipulation primitives—such as grasping a mug or pulling a drawer—are self-evident from geometric affordances. Crucially, all manipulation tasks depend on an indispensable stage: Contact Establishment. By disrupting the initial moment of stable physical engagement between gripper and object, all subsequent downstream execution stages are compromised.

### 3.2 CMP Attack to Robotic Manipulation
The objective is to maximize the attack success rate $\mathrm{ASR}(C')$. This introduces a delicate trade-off between stealth and harm. If the mesh distortion is excessively aggressive, policy training will fail to converge within simulation environment $\mathcal{E}(C')$, tipping off the developer to discard the asset. Conversely, if the alteration is too subtle, the policy generalizes successfully even in normal environment $\mathcal{E}(C)$, failing to cause damage. The authors decompose the attack objective as:

$$\mathrm{ASR}(C') = \mathrm{Stealth}(C') \times \mathrm{Harm}(C')$$

Here, $\mathrm{Stealth}(C')$ represents the policy success rate inside the poisoned simulator, while $\mathrm{Harm}(C')$ measures the fraction of successful poisoned episodes that fail when evaluated on the genuine geometry. The goal of CMP is to discover a collision mesh $C'$ that maximizes the product of both terms.

sections.heading: Gradient-Free Black-Box Optimization: Proxy Scripts and CMA-ES
sections.summary: This section explains the CMP search pipeline, which couples policy-agnostic proxy scripts for rapid candidate scoring with handle-based RBF deformation to respect physics engine constraints. CMA-ES optimizes the non-differentiable simulation outcomes efficiently.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Overview & 4.2 Collision Mesh Parameterization
To maximize the objective function without knowing the victim's policy, the authors constructed a simulator-in-the-loop black-box framework. Directly modifying raw collision meshes violates manifold and convexity criteria, triggering physics engine crashes. Instead, the framework deforms a copy of the visual mesh and applies approximate convex decomposition (CoACD) to synthesize candidate mesh $C'$.

Directly perturbing all vertices is computationally intractable and produces spiky, unnatural geometry. Therefore, the search parameterizes the displacement $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times 3}$ of $k$ control handles $\mathcal{H}$ chosen via Farthest Point Sampling (FPS). Displacements are propagated smoothly across the entire mesh using Radial Basis Functions (RBF) and scaled to ensure average displacement stays within budget $\tau$.

### 4.3 Policy-Agnostic Evaluation
Training reinforcement learning policies from scratch for every candidate mesh is computationally infeasible. To bypass this, the authors implemented deterministic, scripted proxies. For grasping tasks, antipodal grasp poses are sampled from the deformed mesh surface, executing a canonical trajectory: linear approach $\to$ gripper close $\to$ lift. Stealth is estimated by the fraction of successful grasps in $\mathcal{E}(C')$, while Harm is estimated by replaying those successful grasps in normal environment $\mathcal{E}(C)$ and recording failure rates. Leveraging parallel simulation allows candidate scoring without policy training.

### 4.4 Black-box Optimization
Because simulator task outcomes are discrete and non-differentiable, CMA-ES (Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy) is used for optimization. Each iteration samples displacement vectors and updates the distribution toward higher proxy scores $\widehat{\mathrm{ASR}}$. Once iterations conclude, the highest-scoring candidate is packaged into the final poisoned asset.

captions.F3: CMP poisoned 3D asset generation pipeline: (a) formulating the dual objectives of stealth and harm, (b) selecting control handle points via farthest point sampling, (c) generating collision meshes through RBF deformation and convex decomposition, and (d) conducting simulator evaluation using scripted proxies optimized via CMA-ES.

sections.heading: Simulation Results: Stealthy Convergence and Surgical Harm
sections.summary: CMP was evaluated on three benchmarks: YCB object grasping, drawer opening, and cube lift-and-transport. The attack matched clean baseline success rates in simulation while drastically dropping performance in clean environments, demonstrating tight target specificity.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup & Metrics
Evaluations were conducted using PPO (reinforcement learning) across three representative tasks. Key metrics include PSSR (Poisoned Simulation Success Rate, reflecting stealth visible to developers), BSSR (success rate of the poisoned policy in a clean environment), and Drop (the performance drop from the clean baseline BSR minus BSSR, reflecting physical harm).

### 5.2 Main Results
- **Task 1 (YCB Object Grasping)**: Across 9 objects, the average PSSR reached 89.09%, matching the clean baseline BSR of 88.57% and demonstrating remarkable stealth. However, when deployed to clean environments, success dropped severely, showing an average Drop of 56.09 percentage points (reaching an 83.45 point drop for the sugar box).
- **Target Specificity in Multi-Asset Training**: When a single policy was trained on five objects simultaneously with only one object poisoned, performance drops were heavily concentrated on the target object (diagonal, average Drop of 42.6 points), while non-target objects remained largely unaffected (off-diagonal, average Drop of 4.9 points). This proves CMP can selectively disrupt targeted assets without inducing broad training anomalies.
- **Task 2 (Drawer Opening) & Task 3 (Cube Transport)**: Modifying only the drawer handle mesh preserved 100.00% PSSR while achieving a 100.00 point Drop (0% BSSR), representing complete task destruction. For geometrically simplistic shapes like the cube, the Drop was limited to 26.32 points, indicating that basic geometries are more forgiving of contact discrepancies.

### 5.3 & 5.4 Generalization & Proxy Validation
Poisoned assets maintained their attack potency when evaluated with alternative robot arms (OpenArm, AgileX PiPER), across different RL libraries (RL-Games, SKRL), and within entirely different simulators. Additionally, the correlation between scripted proxy scores and actual trained policy degradation yielded a Spearman rank correlation coefficient of 1.00, validating the proxy's predictive power.

captions.F5: Confusion matrix illustrating target specificity in multi-asset grasping. Each cell shows the performance degradation (Drop, in points). Only the targeted asset (diagonal) suffers a steep 40–55 point collapse, while non-target assets (off-diagonal) experience negligible impact.

sections.heading: Physical Franka Panda Validation: Real-World Harm Confirmed
sections.summary: To confirm whether simulation findings translate to reality, experiments were conducted using a physical Franka Panda robot and 3D-printed replicas. While clean policies succeeded 93.33% of the time, poisoned policies succeeded only 31.67%, confirming a ~62-point collapse.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Control Protocol
To evaluate real-world impact, three objects (sugar box, mustard bottle, mug) were 3D-printed with 40% PLA infill directly from original YCB scans. A physical Franka Panda robot was utilized, directly deploying policy weights trained in simulation.

In real environments, standard Sim-to-Real gaps arise from sensory noise and pose estimation errors. To isolate whether failures stemmed strictly from CMP, the authors adopted a controlled execution protocol placing objects at calibrated initial poses via eye-in-hand calibration. Across 20 distinct poses per object, 3 trials each were executed, totaling 360 physical robot trials (2 policies $\times$ 3 objects $\times$ 20 poses $\times$ 3 trials).

### Physical Evaluation Findings
The clean policy achieved an average Base Real-world Success Rate (BRSR) of 93.33%, securing over 85% accuracy across all objects. In contrast, the poisoned policy attained a Poisoned Real-world Success Rate (PRSR) of only 31.67%. The physical performance degradation (Real-World Drop) averaged 61.67 percentage points, demonstrating that the failure modes observed in simulation transfer directly to physical hardware. Observed failures included grippers knocking objects over upon premature contact or dropping them midway through lifting.

sections.heading: Can Existing Defenses Stop It? Geometric and VLM Inspection Limits
sections.summary: The authors tested geometric statistical discrepancy tests alongside visual screening using cutting-edge VLMs such as GPT-4o, GPT-5, and Qwen3-VL. Because legitimate assets already feature high V–C gaps, screening methods struggle to suppress false alarms without letting poisoned meshes slip through.
sections.details:
### 7.1 Statistical Feature-Based Detection
A straightforward defense is statistically flagging geometric deviations between visual and collision meshes. The authors tested four metrics: Volumetric IoU, Normalized Chamfer Distance (NCD), Normalized 95% Hausdorff Distance (NHD95), and Bounding Box Size Difference. When calibrating detection thresholds to keep the False Positive Rate (FPR) around 5% on benign assets, every metric missed at least 6 out of 9 poisoned assets. Because legitimate assets already incorporate extensive geometric simplifications for physics performance, distinguishing malicious deformation from benign optimization via static geometric thresholds is fundamentally challenging.

### 7.2 Automated Visual Inspection
Next, the authors evaluated state-of-the-art multimodal vision-language models (GPT-5, GPT-4o, Qwen3-VL) to visually inspect and compare rendered mesh pairs. While GPT-5 and Qwen3-VL successfully flagged 7 of 9 poisoned assets, they misclassified 41 and 43 of 78 benign assets as anomalous, resulting in excessive false positives. GPT-4o caught only 4 poisoned assets while falsely flagging 66 benign ones. Currently, VLMs lack the contextual domain awareness needed to judge reasonable simplification tolerances in robotics simulation.

### 7.3 Other Defenses
Manual human inspection cannot scale to modern simulation ecosystems housing thousands of assets. Meanwhile, forcing simulators to automatically regenerate collision meshes from scratch frequently destroys delicate task-relevant contact features, degrading training performance on clean assets.

sections.heading: A Hard-to-Detect Blind Spot and Recommendations for the Ecosystem
sections.summary: This section examines why CMP has stayed hidden—primarily due to developers mistaking failures for normal Sim-to-Real divergence—and presents study limitations along with essential security recommendations.
sections.details:
### Why Has This Remained Undetected?
The authors highlight two key structural blind spots explaining why CMP has evaded discovery in the wild. First, developers and platform maintainers focus almost exclusively on visual rendering, leaving underlying collision geometry files uninspected. Second, when a poisoned policy fails on physical hardware, robotics practitioners typically attribute the collapse to standard Sim-to-Real gap issues or insufficient domain randomization, rarely suspecting deliberate mesh tampering.

### Recommendations and Limitations
This study proves that asset supply chain auditing must expand beyond traditional malware and copyright checks to include physical-layer integrity. Simulators should also enhance transparency, such as generating automated warnings whenever third-party collision meshes are loaded.

Study limitations include the reliance on 3D-printed materials rather than native industrial object properties, the omission of extreme hazardous scenarios due to safety constraints, and the lack of an off-the-shelf automated defense. In accordance with responsible disclosure practices, the authors notified affected simulator developers while withholding proprietary platform identities and specific optimization parameters.

sections.heading: Appendix: Evolution of Poisoned Meshes and Physical Setup Details
sections.summary: The appendix provides supplementary context, including visualizations of collision mesh evolution across CMA-ES iterations, formal mathematical definitions of geometric metrics, and safety protocols used in physical experiments.
sections.details:
### Poisoned Mesh Evolution (Appendix C)
Visualizations show collision contact boundaries progressively hollowing and distorting across CMA-ES iterations (iteration 10, iteration 20, and final candidate). While the visual mesh remains pristine, the collision mesh morphs into a delicate shape that barely satisfies scripted grasps in simulation while ensuring consistent drops or collisions under true geometry.

### Definitions of Geometric Metrics (Appendix D)
Formal formulations are provided for the four geometric metrics evaluated in the defense section: Volumetric IoU, Normalized Chamfer Distance (NCD) averaging nearest-neighbor distances across uniformly sampled surface points, Normalized 95% Hausdorff Distance (NHD95) capturing localized surface deviations, and Bounding Box Size Difference.

### Physical Experiment Safety Protocols (Appendix B)
Hardware trials were conducted using 40% PLA infill printed objects, with an emergency stop button actively held by trained operators at all times. Controlled experimental safeguards ensured zero risk of injury or equipment damage throughout physical validation.

captions.F10: Evolutionary optimization of poisoned collision meshes for the cracker box, sugar box, and tomato soup can. While the visual meshes on the far left stay untouched, collision meshes smoothly distort across iterations, forming deceptive contact boundaries.

takeaways: High simulation success is no longer a guarantee of real-world reliability: corrupted collision meshes bypass simulation benchmarks while triggering complete failure on physical hardware.
Freely downloaded 3D models from open platforms carry significant supply chain risks; visually authentic assets can conceal maliciously deformed physical collision boundaries.
Attackers do not need access to victim RL algorithms or policy architectures; policy-agnostic proxy scripts and CMA-ES can automatically generate highly potent poisoned meshes.

Defending against CMP is difficult because legitimate assets already feature pronounced Visual–Collision gaps for physics efficiency, causing standard geometric thresholds and modern VLMs to trigger overwhelming false positive rates.
limitations: Real-world experiments relied on 3D-printed plastic objects under open-loop grasp execution; verifying attacks under diverse real-world materials and dynamic closed-loop visual feedback remains future work.
While devastating for contact-establishment tasks (e.g., grasping and drawer pulling), the attack is less effective against contact-avoidance tasks such as mobile robot obstacle navigation.
Although the paper thoroughly proves the vulnerability, establishing an automated defense that reliably catches CMP without degrading policy performance on benign assets remains an open challenge.
